quote: I've been interested in, solar for a long time, and a lot of my neighbors have it. And, you know, with this oil business, I thought, well, maybe this is a good time to look into it seriously.
stewart_read: The customer hands over a rich, specific motivator — long-standing interest, neighbor social proof, and a current events trigger ('this oil business') — and the rep's response is a generic acknowledgment before pivoting straight to the roof.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged the customer was already sold and didn't need further emotional building, prioritizing pace instead.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to reflect the specific language back ('so with everything going on with oil prices, you want to lock in your rate now?') to reinforce the customer's own reasoning rather than letting it pass.

quote: So it varies, you know, because we just pay by the month. And so it varies from less than $100 to maybe low 2 hundreds tops.
stewart_read: The rep captured a bill range but the number given here later turns out to be inaccurate due to the billing dispute — this early anchor gets overtaken by events, but the rep never returns to it once the real numbers surface.
coaching_implication: No major issue here since the real usage data was captured later, but flag that the rep never re-anchored emotionally once the true magnitude of the bill (over $1,000 back-charged) became clear.

quote: But, you know, I have a problem with the bill. Excel messed up. So they installed a new, like, measuring device outside on the side of my house, and they inadvertently... I have the same address as a neighbor around the corner.
stewart_read: Customer discloses a fairly involved billing dispute; the rep listens but offers no acknowledgment of the frustration this likely caused before moving straight to a workaround ('if you have the last three or four that were accurate').
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged this as an operational problem, not an emotional one, and correctly triaged it to a practical fix rather than dwelling on it.
coaching_implication: A brief empathy line ('that's frustrating, glad you got it sorted') costs nothing and would have matched the vulnerability_disclosure principle before pivoting to the practical ask.

quote: I just got a bill for $584. And I wonder what so I think that's probably they're back charging me. Yeah. Because amount due, $1,039.26.
stewart_read: A $1,039 amount due — driven partly by a real ongoing bill, not just back-charges — is a striking number that lands live on the call, and the rep's response is a flat acknowledgment ('Oh, wow. Okay. Gotcha.') rather than using the number as leverage for urgency.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have deliberately not pushed on the number because the customer had already framed it as a billing error rather than his real ongoing cost, making it a poor anchor to lean on emotionally.
coaching_implication: Even flagging it lightly — 'that's exactly the kind of bill swing solar protects you from' — would have tied the moment to value without needing to dwell on the disputed portion.

stewart_read: Rep offers a clean choice-based path for bill collection and follows the schema's branching logic well, giving the customer control over method.
coaching_implication: This is a positive example worth reinforcing — no coaching correction needed, just note it as a strength.

quote: Yeah. I know usage. Usage. Oh, it's usage. Let me try that. History. Yeah. That would be perfect.
stewart_read: Rep stayed with a customer who was struggling to navigate the utility portal, coaching him step by step for roughly two minutes rather than abandoning the ask, which aligns with the schema's guidance to pivot but not give up on bill capture.
alternative_hypothesis: A reactive read would call this a time-burn since it took several minutes, but the schema explicitly rewards persistence on paid-lead bill capture over speed, and the rep got a full six months of usage data as a result.
coaching_implication: Reinforce this patience as a model for other reps handling low-tech customers, distinct from calls where reps burn 10+ minutes with no result.

quote: Okay. Thank you, Parker. Of course. Hey. You have a great day, William. Thanks for your time.
